# Reproducibility as a Discipline: Every Number in This Project, Rerunnable

### If a claim can't be regenerated by rerunning a script against the same source file, it doesn't get published as VERIFIED

A number in a research write-up is either something you can check or something you have to take on faith. This project aims to minimize the second kind.

## What "reproducible" means here, concretely

Every VERIFIED-tier claim in this project traces back to a specific script, in the repository, that anyone can run against the same publicly described raw data structure to get the same result. A file with the logic, in `/analysis`, produces the number when executed.

This shapes how the work is done. A finding that can only be produced by manual spreadsheet manipulation, eyeballing, or a one-off interactive session that wasn't saved as a script doesn't get to carry the VERIFIED label, because nobody, including this project's own author, a month later, could actually rerun it to check.

## The discipline this creates

Writing a script instead of doing ad-hoc analysis is slower in the moment. It is also the way to catch your own mistakes before publishing them. A script's logic can be read, questioned, and re-run with a fix; a half-remembered manual process can't. Several of this project's own corrections, documented elsewhere in this series, were caught specifically because a script existed to rerun.

## Why this matters more for surprising numbers

People rarely double-check numbers that confirm what they expected. The temptation to skip verification is strongest when a finding is most attention-grabbing: the biggest anomaly, the most damning ratio, the best headline. A rerunnable script matters most then, because it separates "this looks alarming" from "this is alarming and also correct."

## What this is, and isn't

**A standing practice, not a claim about any single number**: every script behind a VERIFIED claim in this project is in the public repository, with its inputs and logic visible.

**A limit**: reproducibility shows the computation is correct given the input. It doesn't verify that the underlying raw data itself is accurate or complete. That's a separate, STATED-tier question about the data's own provenance.

Full script index: **github.com/DreamITSoftware/SPOTAPOD**.

> **Update, 22 October 2026.** The figures drawn from the [65 export files](../provenance.md#the-65-export-files) follow this rule. `export65_profile.py` produces the file-level figures, and the shared reader `export65_loader.py` lets the existing content scans run on the files. The files are not in the repository, and `--check-manifest` compares a folder of files against `checksums/EXPORT65_MANIFEST.csv`. The limit stated above applies in full: the source and method of the files are the collector's account (STATED).
